# Add Projections to CI

This file guides you, a coding agent, to add the Projections GitHub Action to this repository’s CI, so every pull request and push summarizes how its projections changed and uploads them as an artifact. Where the step belongs depends on the repository’s CI, so no command writes it: you read the workflows, reason about where it fits, and propose the change for the person to approve.

## Your task

1. Check that the repository defines at least one projection: `projections list`. If it defines none, say so and stop: they are adopted with `projections explore` and `projections adopt`, or built with `projections init`. Note which projections it says run repository code (they need `trust: true`), and run `projections doctor` for the toolchains and prepare steps their extractors use.
2. Read every workflow in `.github/workflows/`: its triggers, default branch, runners, matrices, permissions, path filters, and each job’s setup, install and build steps. If one already runs `githubnext/projections`, say so and stop.
3. Decide where the step belongs, as “Where it goes” below explains. The default is a step in the job that already sets up the toolchains and installs the dependencies (in a repository with one build, test and lint workflow, that job), after its install and build steps, so nothing is installed twice.
4. Propose a workflow of its own only when no job sets up what the extractors need, every projection only reads files, or the job can’t take the step.
5. Adapt the step to that job: change its checkout to `fetch-depth: 0` and `persist-credentials: false`; guard the step with `if:` when the workflow runs on events other than `pull_request` and `push`; run it in one matrix entry only; add `working-directory` for a project in a subdirectory.
6. Add `trust: true` only for projections that need it, in a job with read-only permissions and no secrets. Check what the checkout change affects, such as a later step that pushes with the checkout’s credentials, and pick the narrowest fix.
7. Show the person the diff and why you chose that place over the alternatives, including what it costs (a full-history checkout, a step before or after the tests) and what a pull request installs (below). Write it only once they agree; never change CI on your own.
8. Commit only if they ask. After the change is merged, the default branch’s next push run produces the artifact that pull requests reuse for their merge base.

Once you've [adopted](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/setup/quick-start.md#step-3-adopt-the-useful-ones) the
projections worth keeping, wire them into CI so every pull request and push gets
a summary of what changed—without anyone needing to run anything locally. All it
takes is one step in your workflow using the Projections GitHub Action. It
writes the summary to the workflow run (and optionally posts a pull request
comment) and uploads the projection documents as an artifact that you can
[review locally or in a hosted view](#reviewing-the-results).

Because the best place for that step depends on how your CI is set up, nothing
modifies your workflows automatically. Instead, paste this prompt into your
coding agent—it reads your workflows, suggests where the step belongs, and shows
you the diff before writing anything:

In VS Code, clicking **Add to CI…** in the Explore view (or running
**Projections: Add to CI…**) sends the same prompt to your agent or opens this
page. If you'd rather wire it up yourself, read on.

## The step

```yaml
- uses: githubnext/projections@v0
```

Make sure the job checks out full history and doesn't persist credentials:

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@v6
  with:
    fetch-depth: 0 # both the merge base and the head must be in the checkout
    persist-credentials: false # extractors never see the token
```

Here's why each setting matters:

- **`fetch-depth: 0`** ensures both the merge base and head commits (and the
  history between them) are present. A shallow checkout fails with
  `Commit … is not in the checkout`. The only downside is a slightly slower
  checkout in very large repositories.
- **`persist-credentials: false`** keeps the token out of `.git/config` so no
  repository code running in the job can read it. This is required when using
  [`trust: true`](#trust), which runs code from the pull request. Without trust,
  the Action doesn't execute repository code, so it adds no new exposure beyond
  your existing steps.
- **Events:** the Action runs on `pull_request` and `push`. Any other event
  (`merge_group`, `workflow_dispatch`, `schedule`, `release`) fails the step,
  and `pull_request_target` is rejected outright because it would run pull
  request code with the base repository's secrets. Run it on pushes to your
  default branch as well as pull requests so pull requests can reuse the merge
  base's artifact instead of re-extracting it (see
  [what a pull request installs](#what-a-pull-request-installs)).
- **Permissions:** `contents: read` is all you need, since uploading an artifact
  requires no extra permission. See [Permissions](#permissions) if you turn on
  features that write back to the repository or pull request.

The Action automatically runs every projection defined in your repository, so
adopting more projections later requires no CI changes.

## Where it goes

In most repositories, **adding the step to the job that already builds your
code** is the best fit. If you have a single CI workflow that installs
dependencies, builds, tests, and lints, your toolchains and packages are already
in place there—a separate workflow would repeat that expensive setup. Drop the
step in after install and build, update that job's checkout as shown above, and
guard the step if the workflow also triggers on other events:

```yaml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  merge_group:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0 # added for Projections
          persist-credentials: false # added for Projections
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version-file: .node-version
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: githubnext/projections@v0 # added: after the build, before the tests
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.event_name == 'push'
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
```

A few things to keep in mind when adding it to an existing job:

- **Before or after the tests:** because a failing step skips everything after
  it, placing Projections after the build and before tests ensures projections
  still get reported when a test fails. Putting it at the end waits for tests
  and skips on failure—unless you combine your event guard with
  `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}`.
- **Steps that modify tracked files:** on a push, the Action extracts the
  checked-out commit in place, reusing your installed dependencies and build
  artifacts as long as tracked files haven't been altered (untracked and ignored
  files like `node_modules` and `dist` are fine). Place it ahead of any step
  that rewrites tracked files, such as an auto-formatter or version bumper.
- **Steps that push:** setting `persist-credentials: false` will break any step
  that commits or pushes using the checkout's saved credentials. The cleanest
  fix is to pass a token directly to that step (for example, pushing with
  `git push` to `https://x-access-token:${{ github.token }}@github.com/…`, or
  passing a `token` input to an action). If the job doesn't need
  [trust](#trust), you can leave checkout credentials enabled; otherwise, move
  Projections into its own job.
- **Matrix jobs:** running the step in every matrix cell causes each one to
  upload an artifact with the same name, which fails. Restrict it to a single
  cell (for example, `if: matrix.os == 'ubuntu-latest' && matrix.node == 24`) or
  run it in a non-matrix job.
- **Multiple workflows:** pick the job whose environment matches what your
  extractors need. Run `projections list` to see which projections execute
  repository code (and therefore need [trust](#trust)), and `projections doctor`
  to see the toolchains and declared prepare steps they use. File-only
  extractors need no toolchain setup at all, so they work in any job or in their
  own workflow.
- **Monorepo projects:** for a project living in a subdirectory, set
  `working-directory` to that path inside the job that builds it.

If no existing job sets up what your extractors need, if every projection only
reads files, or if your build job can't accommodate the step (for instance, it
pushes and requires trust), give Projections **a workflow of its own** at
`.github/workflows/projections.yml`:

```yaml
name: Projections
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  projections:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0 # both the merge base and the head must be in the checkout
          persist-credentials: false # extractors never see the token
      - uses: githubnext/projections@v0
```

Adjust the default branch, runner (`runs-on`), and path filters to match your
repo. If any projection needs your toolchain, add the required setup and install
steps ahead of the Projections step, or declare them as
[prepare steps](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/runner/environments.md) in
`.github/projections/environment.json`.

## What a pull request installs

On a pull request, the Action compares the merge base against the pull request
head. Neither of those is the synthetic merge commit that `actions/checkout`
checks out (`refs/pull/<number>/merge`), so each side is handled slightly
differently:

- **The merge base** is reused instead of re-extracted whenever the merge base's
  own CI run succeeded and uploaded a `projections` artifact (typically from the
  push run on your default branch). Only a run from the same workflow file in
  this repository for a push or in-repo pull request qualifies—a fork's pull
  request runs its own workflow files, so its artifacts are never reused. The
  Action downloads the artifact and the CLI verifies each extraction, marking it
  as imported rather than official because the CLI step has no token to
  authenticate it. That's why it helps to run the step on pushes to the default
  branch in a passing run, and why `retention-days` matters.
- **File-only projections** read both commits directly from Git objects without
  installing anything.
- **Toolchain projections** (running with [trust](#trust)) need each commit
  checked out on disk, so the CLI extracts them in a temporary copy. If you
  haven't declared prepare steps, that copy borrows the dependencies your job
  already installed—exact when the commit's lockfiles match the checkout, or
  labelled _approximate_ (listing which lockfiles differ) when they don't. Build
  output isn't copied over. If you declare
  [prepare steps](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/runner/environments.md), the copy runs them instead to
  produce a clean install for each extracted commit.

In the typical case, adding the step to your build job avoids any extra
installs: the merge base comes from the default branch's artifact, and the head
borrows the job's dependencies (whose lockfiles match the head unless the base
branch also changed them). If a pull request edits a lockfile and its merge base
has no cached artifact, the base is labelled _approximate_ rather than
triggering a fresh install; declare prepare steps if you'd rather pay for that
install than see the label. On a push, the checkout already is the target
commit, so it's extracted in place with everything the job set up.

## How it compares

On `pull_request`, the Action runs
`projections compare --all <merge-base>..<head> --definition base --json`,
comparing the merge base to the head using the base branch's projection
definitions (just like a local `projections compare`). On `push`, it extracts
every projection for the pushed commit with
`projections show --all <commit> --json`. In both cases, it uploads one document
per projection along with a `projections.artifact.json` manifest as an Actions
artifact named `projections` (see the
[artifact contract](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/contracts/saved-documents.md#ci-artifacts)).

Before running anything, the Action downloads the matching CLI binary for the
runner's OS and architecture from GitHub Releases and verifies both its
`.sha256` digest and its build provenance attestation via
`gh attestation verify`. By default, it picks the CLI release matching the
Action's version tag: `@v0.1.0` installs v0.1.0, and `@v0` tracks the latest
stable v0 release without jumping to v1. Each stable release advances its major
tag (`v0`), while pinning a commit SHA, branch, or `@latest` installs the latest
release.

<!-- prettier-ignore -->
| Input | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `trust` | `false` | Pass `--trust`, so extractors that run repository code run. See below. |
| `summary` | `true` | Write each projection's result, steps and changes to the job summary. |
| `comment` | `false` | Also post the summary as one pull request comment, updated on each run. Needs `pull-requests: write`. |
| `retention-days` | repository default | How long GitHub keeps the artifact. |
| `attest` | `false` | Attest the artifact's manifest with [GitHub artifact attestations](#attesting-the-artifact). Needs `id-token: write` and `attestations: write`. |
| `fail-on-error` | `false` | Fail the job when a projection fails. By default failures are reported per projection, in the summary and as annotations, and the job succeeds. |
| `snapshots` | none | Projection IDs to render as PNG [snapshots](#snapshots), light and dark. |
| `snapshots-commit`, `snapshots-path` | `false`, `.github/projections/snapshots` | On pushes to the default branch, commit the snapshots for embedding in a README. Needs `contents: write`. |
| `snapshots-branch` | none | On pull requests from this repository, commit the before and after snapshots to this dedicated branch so the comment shows them. Needs `contents: write`. |
| `version` | the Action's version | A CLI release such as `v0.1.0`, a major version such as `v0` (its newest stable release), or `latest`. |
| `build-from-source` | `false` | Build the CLI from the Action's source instead (needs Rust), for testing unreleased versions. |
| `working-directory`, `artifact-name`, `hosted-url`, `token`, `cli-repository` | | Less common settings, documented in `action.yml`. |

## Permissions

On its own, the step only needs `contents: read`—uploading an artifact needs no
extra permission. Add `pull-requests: write` only if you enable `comment: true`,
and `contents: write` only for `snapshots-commit` or `snapshots-branch`. When
editing an existing workflow, scope `permissions:` to that specific job rather
than the entire workflow. If you enable `trust: true`, keep the job restricted
to read-only permissions and no secrets (see [Trust](#trust)). Pull requests
from forks never receive a writable token, so they won't get a PR comment,
though their job summary and artifact are still generated.

### Attesting the artifact

Turning on `attest: true` uses `actions/attest` to attest
`projections.artifact.json`, which records the SHA-256 of every document in the
artifact. Anyone downloading that artifact can then authenticate it: running
`projections show <commit> --ci --artifact DIR` verifies the manifest with
`gh attestation verify` and treats it as the commit's official extraction only
if the attestation points to a run of this repository's Projections workflow on
a push or an in-repo pull request. Without an attestation, an imported directory
is still reusable, just labelled imported.

Attestation requires `id-token: write` and `attestations: write` on the job, and
the repository must have artifact attestations available (all public
repositories, or private repositories on GitHub Enterprise Cloud). Fork pull
requests skip attestation because they don't receive an `id-token` and aren't
the repository's own CI output.

## Snapshots

Passing `snapshots` tells the Action to render the listed projections into light
and dark PNG images using the real renderer via
[`projections show --png`](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/runner/commands.md#images) and the runner's
installed Chrome (GitHub-hosted runners include Chrome; set `browser` if yours
doesn't). It renders straight from the documents it just collected without
re-running extractors, and the render step receives no token.

Pushes produce `<id>.light.png` and `<id>.dark.png` for the pushed commit, while
pull requests produce `<id>.before.<theme>.png` (merge base) and
`<id>.after.<theme>.png` (head). The images and a `snapshots.json` index are
uploaded in a separate `projections-snapshots` artifact so the `projections`
artifact matches its manifest exactly. Snapshot failures are logged as warnings
and never fail the job. Because a custom renderer is repository code, snapshots
only use it when `trust: true` is set; otherwise they fall back to the built-in
renderer for that schema and log a note.

```yaml
permissions:
  contents: write       # snapshots-commit and snapshots-branch
  pull-requests: write  # comment
# …
      - uses: githubnext/projections@v0
        with:
          snapshots: architecture, files
          snapshots-commit: true                # pushes to the default branch
          snapshots-branch: projections-snapshots # pull request comments
          comment: true
```

**Embedding in a README.** With `snapshots-commit: true`, pushes to the default
branch commit any changed images to `snapshots-path` (by default
`.github/projections/snapshots`) through the GitHub API, similar to the original
repo-visualizer Action's `should_push`. Unchanged images don't create empty
commits, nothing is pushed if the branch moved in the meantime, and commits made
with `GITHUB_TOKEN` won't trigger recursive workflows. Embed them with a picture
element so they adapt to the reader's theme:

```html
<picture>
  <source
    media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"
    srcset=".github/projections/snapshots/files.dark.png"
  />
  <img
    alt="Repository files"
    src=".github/projections/snapshots/files.light.png"
  />
</picture>
```

**Showing in pull request comments.** Because GitHub comments can't render
Actions artifacts inline, setting `snapshots-branch` commits an in-repo pull
request's images under `pull/<number>/` on a dedicated orphan branch (created
automatically if missing, and never your base or head branch). The comment then
embeds theme-aware before-and-after thumbnails pinned to that commit. Readers
need read access to the repository, just as they do for the code. Fork pull
requests receive a read-only token, and without `snapshots-branch` nothing is
committed—in both cases, the comment links to the snapshots artifact instead.
The branch accumulates commits as images change, and you can delete it anytime
to start fresh.

## Reviewing the results

- **In the job summary:** every run reports what was compared (a pull request's
  merge base and head, or the pushed commit) and lists each projection's
  outcome. For each comparison, it walks through the changes in the comparator's
  order—listing each step in plain language (`Added entity …`,
  `Renamed relationship … to …`) along with any comparator summaries. Failed
  projections show diagnostics and appear as workflow annotations. With
  `comment: true`, that same summary (plus any snapshots) is posted and updated
  as a single pull request comment.
- **Locally from the pull request:** run
  [`projections pr <number>`](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/runner/pull-requests.md) to reproduce a pull
  request's comparisons on your machine—from merge base to head using the base
  definitions—without trusting the PR's code. Pass `--output FILE` to save the
  review for later.
- **In VS Code (alternate path):** if you use the VS Code extension, download
  and unzip the `projections` artifact, then open `projections/<id>.json` with
  **Projections: Open Artifact…** (or from the Explorer context menu). It
  displays the saved extraction or comparison without executing anything; any
  provenance (including whether it claims to be official) comes from the
  document itself.
- **In a hosted view:** because the artifact adheres to a
  [documented contract](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/contracts/saved-documents.md#ci-artifacts), external
  services can render it too. Set `hosted-url` to that service's origin (for
  example, `https://projections.example`), and both the job summary and pull
  request comment will link straight to its view of the pull request or commit.

## Trust

The Action enforces the same [trust rule](https://github.com/githubnext/projections/blob/main/docs/guides/how-it-works.md#trust) as
the CLI. Built-in extractors that only read files always run. Custom extractors
and built-in extractors that invoke your toolchain require `trust: true`;
without it, they appear as failed projections explaining why they were skipped.
Custom renderers are repository code as well, so [snapshots](#snapshots) only
use them when `trust: true` is enabled.

On a pull request, `trust: true` runs code from the pull request's head in CI.
Only enable it on the standard `pull_request` event (never
`pull_request_target`), with no secrets, read-only permissions, and
`persist-credentials: false`—matching how GitHub already isolates workflows for
fork pull requests. If a build job already runs tests on pull requests, it
already executes pull request code, so adding Projections there with
`trust: true` stays within the same trust boundary. Reading the resulting
artifact never executes repository code: the job summary, **Projections: Open
Artifact…**, and hosted views only display saved documents.
